item.title: Child protection must come before racial divisions – Ro Naulu
item.description: The safety of Fiji's children must come before racial differences and political disagreements, with Great Council of Chiefs member Ro Naulu Mataitini calling on traditional leaders and communities to work together to protect children from abuse, violence and neglect. Ro Naulu made the comments in a personal statement following social media criticism of Minister for Women, Children, Social Protecti
item.content:encoded:
The safety of Fiji's children must come before racial differences and political disagreements, with Great Council of Chiefs member Ro Naulu Mataitini calling on traditional leaders and communities to work together to protect children from abuse, violence and neglect.

Ro Naulu made the comments in a personal statement following social media criticism of Minister for Women, Children, Social Protection and Cohesion Sashi Kiran's address to the Great Council of Chiefs on Thursday.

He says some people questioned why an Indo-Fijian woman was allowed to address the Council, while others claimed she did not represent them.

However, Ro Naulu says the focus should be on the serious issues Kiran raised, including child sexual abuse, violence, drugs, neglect and the long-term effects of childhood trauma.

He stresses that these problems affect children from all communities, regardless of their race or background.

Ro Naulu says a child who suffers abuse does not experience pain differently because of their ethnicity.

He says it is concerning that some people appear more focused on the platform from which Kiran delivered her message than on the suffering of the children she spoke about.

Ro Naulu says traditional leaders have an important responsibility to protect children because their influence extends to villages, districts and communities across Fiji.

He says while laws, police and social workers play important roles, changing attitudes and behaviour also requires the involvement of families, churches and traditional leaders.

Ro Naulu str esses that chiefs must ensure traditional customs are never used to shield people accused of child abuse.

He says traditional reconciliation must not interfere with police investigations or prevent victims from speaking out, adding that a traditional apology does not remove a person's responsibility under the law.

He is calling for stronger child protection measures in village by-laws, improved reporting systems and greater support for vulnerable parents.

Ro Naulu say s chiefs must help create communities where children feel safe to speak out and where those responsible for abuse cannot use their status or family connections to avoid accountability.

He also defended Kiran's engagement with the Great Council of Chiefs, saying she has a responsibility to protect all women and children in Fiji, regardless of ethnicity.

Ro Naulu says w orking with traditional leaders does not mean a person has to give up their identity, beliefs or right to criticise an institution.

He acknowledges that both iTaukei and Indo-Fijian communities have experienced historical injustices but says these should not prevent people from working together to address issues affecting Fiji today.

Ro Naulu says Fiji cannot continue calling for unity while criticising those making an effort to bring communities together.

He stresses that protecting children should be one issue on which all communities can agree.

He is urging traditional leaders and those who criticised Kiran to reflect on whether their actions are helping protect Fiji's children or continuing divisions between communities.

He says children deserve better than to inherit the divisions of previous generations and the failure of adults to work together to protect them.

item.title: Small yaqona farmers could face $10,000 fines under proposed Yaqona Bill – SEEP
item.description: Small yaqona farmers who rely on kava sales for their livelihoods could face fines of up to $10,000 or two years' imprisonment for operating without the required registration or licence under the proposed Yaqona Bill 2026, according to concerns raised by the Social Empowerment Education Programme (SEEP). SEEP raised the concerns in its submission to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Justice,
item.content:encoded:
Small yaqona farmers who rely on kava sales for their livelihoods could face fines of up to $10,000 or two years' imprisonment for operating without the required registration or licence under the proposed Yaqona Bill 2026, according to concerns raised by the Social Empowerment Education Programme (SEEP).

SEEP raised the concerns in its submission to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Justice, Law and Human Rights, warning that the proposed legislation could place an unfair burden on small-scale farmers and traders.

The organisation says small farmers, roadside sellers and people growing yaqona to support their families could be subjected to the same regulatory requirements as large commercial exporters.

SEEP says this could create additional challenges for ordinary farmers who depend on yaqona sales as their main source of income.

According to the 2024 National Yaqona Farming Household Census, Fiji has 14,532 yaqona farming households and 17,200 farmers.

SEEP says approximately 93 percent of these households rely on yaqona as their main source of income, highlighting the importance of protecting their livelihoods.

The organisation is calling for exemptions for small-scale farmers from certain requirements under the proposed law, as well as penalties that reflect the size and nature of farming operations.

They are also recommending that farmers be given warnings, assistance and adequate time to comply with the requirements before penalties are imposed.

SEEP has raised concerns that some farmers and market vendors were unaware of the public consultations on the Bill.

They are calling for the consultation period to be extended from 30 to 60 days to allow more farmers, particularly those in rural and maritime communities, to have their say.

The organisation also wants small-scale farmers, women, young people and maritime communities to be represented in the proposed Fiji Yaqona Council and Yaqona Working Group.

SEEP is further recommending the introduction of a yaqona tracking system to help address theft, along with more accessible registration services for farmers who have limited access to online facilities.

SEEP Executive Director Chantelle Khan says while regulations are important for the future of Fiji's yaqona industry, they must also protect the people who depend on it for their livelihoods.

Khan says the proposed rules should be fair and developed with the involvement of farmers, women and young people.

She stresses that SEEP is not opposing the regulation of the yaqona industry but wants the proposed legislation strengthened to ensure small farmers are not unfairly disadvantaged.

SEEP is urging the Government and the Parliamentary Standing Committee to consider its recommendations before the Bill is finalised.

item.title: New recycling centre to help tackle waste pollution on Taveuni
item.description: Families, schools and businesses on Taveuni are expected to benefit from improved recycling services following the launch of a new waste management initiative aimed at reducing pollution and protecting the island's land and surrounding waters. The Taveuni Waste Management Initiative was officially launched yesterday, bringing together communities, schools, tourism operators, businesses and Governm
item.content:encoded:
Families, schools and businesses on Taveuni are expected to benefit from improved recycling services following the launch of a new waste management initiative aimed at reducing pollution and protecting the island's land and surrounding waters.

The Taveuni Waste Management Initiative was officially launched yesterday, bringing together communities, schools, tourism operators, businesses and Government representatives to strengthen waste management on the island.

The two-and-a-half-year initiative is being implemented by the Pacific Recycling Foundation with support from the CleanSeas programme and other development partners.

Under the initiative, recyclable materials will be collected and transported to the newly established Taveuni Recycling Centre, which will be managed by Nasomo Yalovata Co-operatives Limited.

The collected materials will then be transported to Suva by Ashok Transport for further processing and recycling.

Pacific Recycling Foundation Founder and Director Amitesh Deo says the launch marks only the beginning, with the real work starting as plans are put into action.

Deo says the initiative must respond to the needs of the people and communities of Taveuni, with a focus on developing a recycling system suited to the island.

Meanwhile, Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica says the initiative is an important step towards reducing waste and protecting the environment.

Kamikamica says Taveuni is taking a leading role in Fiji's move towards a society where materials are recovered, recycled and reused rather than simply discarded.

Nasomo Yalovata Co-operatives Limited Taveuni Project Administrative Officer Sakiusa Maiwiliwili says the initiative is a significant development for communities, schools and resorts on the island.

He says the cooperative is committed to the project and looks forward to involving village elders, families and households in recycling activities.

Maiwiliwili says the initiative will allow local communities to play a direct role in protecting Taveuni's environment.

The project will focus on improving waste collection, encouraging community participation and exploring livelihood opportunities through recycling.

GIZ Representative in the South Pacific and Head of the CleanSeas Project Frauke Bartels says preventing rubbish from reaching the ocean begins with better waste management on land.

Bartels says working with local communities, businesses and organisations will help reduce the amount of waste that could end up polluting the sea.

The initiative is funded by the German Government and supported through the CleanSeas programme, in partnership with Fiji's Ministry of Environment and Climate Change.

Over the coming months, the Pacific Recycling Foundation and its partners will work with communities to strengthen recycling activities and help keep Taveuni's land and surrounding waters clean.
